title: Contemplate and share
hookLine: the friars' life: prayer and study fill the basin, and preaching is what spills over

lines: A CHANNEL: ALWAYS FLOWING, NEVER FULL.
A BASIN: FILLS FIRST, THEN SPILLS.
cards: Two ways to move water. A channel takes water in at one end and lets it out the other at the same moment: always flowing, never full. A basin fills first.
It holds the water, and only when it's full to the brim does it spill over the edge, and it stays full while it spills. Bernard of Clairvaux, a Cistercian monk, used this picture in a sermon.

Too many people, he said, are channels; he wished they were basins. Later a Dominican friar put the same idea into a short Latin phrase, and his order took it up as a motto. Today: fill first, then spill.

teach.b: The friar was Thomas Aquinas. In his Summa he asks a practical question: what kind of religious life is best? Pure prayer, hidden away?
Pure action, out in the streets? Neither by itself, he says.
Best is to contemplate, and to hand on to others what you have contemplated. In Latin, contemplari et contemplata aliis tradere.

teach.h: BETTER TO GIVE LIGHT THAN ONLY SHINE.
teach.b: His reason is a lovely image: it is a greater thing to give light than only to shine. A lamp glowing in a closed room is good. A lamp carried into a dark street is better.
That's the Dominican shape of life. The friars pray the hours together in choir. They study.
Then they go out and preach. The preaching isn't meant to be a performance or a sales pitch. It's overflow, the basin spilling over.

teach.h: OUT OF THE ABUNDANCE OF THE HEART.
teach.b: Jesus says something close in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." Whatever fills you is what comes out. But notice the order of the words: contemplate first, then share.
A friar who only talks runs dry; a friar who only prays keeps the light in the closet. The phrase also works as a small test. Before you give advice, have you looked long at the thing?
And after you've looked long, did anyone else get to see it?

how: Dominican friars and sisters pray the Liturgy of the Hours together and set time aside for study, and their preaching and teaching are meant to flow from that prayer; contemplata aliis tradere is quoted as a Dominican motto.

o: pray and look long first, then hand on what you've seen
split each day evenly between prayer and charity work
study theology, then debate it with other scholars

games.q: fill, then spill — tap the pairs.
p: wished people were basins, not channels
a lamp in a dark street

s: the Dominicans are an active order with little time for prayer
the friars pray the hours together and study; preaching is meant to overflow from that.
Aquinas says it's greater to give light than only to shine
his reason for a life that both contemplates and shares.
Bernard's sermon tells people to be channels
he wished they were basins: full first, then spilling over.

games.q: Aquinas asks which religious life is best. which does he choose?
o: pure action, out in the streets.
contemplation that is handed on to others.
games.why: contemplari et contemplata aliis tradere: to contemplate, and to hand on what you contemplated. it is greater, he says, to give light than only to shine.

practice: Look back over this week's quiet moments, a line from a psalm, a thought on a walk, something from one of these sits, and let one come forward: not the most impressive, the one that still feels warm.

Hold it for a few breaths, then bring to mind one person who might need exactly that; if you pray, give thanks for what you received and ask for the right moment to pass it on, and if not, hold the thought and the person side by side.

wordCard.voice: Contemplate and share. Look long at God, then hand on what you've seen: a Dominican motto, from Thomas Aquinas. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from Thomas Aquinas: to hand on to others the things contemplated. a Dominican motto.

carryVoice: Your line: overflow. A basin gives from what it holds, and stays full while it gives. See you tomorrow.
